🚨 KOTAK MAHINDRA BANK JUMPS OVER 3%: RBI APPROVES ANUP KUMAR SAHA AS NEW MD & CEO

Kotak Mahindra Bank shares rallied sharply on October 1 after the private-sector lender announced Anup Kumar Saha as its next Managing Director and CEO, providing clarity on one of the bank's biggest near-term uncertainties: leadership succession.

The stock rose more than 3% in morning trade and was trading around ₹431.20 at 10:18 AM.

THE BIG ANNOUNCEMENT 🏦

🔹 New MD & CEO: Anup Kumar Saha
🔹 RBI approval received
🔹 Term: 3 years
🔹 Effective from: January 1, 2027
🔹 Succeeds: Ashok Vaswani
🔹 Vaswani's current term ends: December 31, 2026
🔹 Shareholder approval will also be sought

The appointment provides a defined succession path after Vaswani decided not to seek another term.

WHO IS ANUP KUMAR SAHA? 👤

Saha joined Kotak Mahindra Bank in January 2026 and currently serves as Whole-Time Director and Executive Director.

At Kotak, he oversees:

🔹 Retail Banking
🔹 Government Business
🔹 Data Analytics
🔹 Marketing

But his previous experience is particularly interesting.

Before joining Kotak, Saha spent more than seven years at Bajaj Finance and eventually became its Managing Director & CEO.

He also spent around 14 years at ICICI Bank in senior leadership roles.

Overall, Saha brings more than three decades of professional experience, with deep exposure to consumer finance, retail banking, analytics and digital transformation.

THE BAJAJ FINANCE CONNECTION 📊

Saha joined Bajaj Finance in 2017 as President of Consumer Finance and subsequently served in several senior positions, including:

🔹 Deputy CEO
🔹 Executive Director
🔹 Deputy Managing Director
🔹 Managing Director & CEO

Kotak had highlighted earlier that during his tenure at Bajaj Finance, Saha played a significant role in scaling the consumer-finance franchise, digital transformation and customer-focused growth.

WHY THE MARKET IS WATCHING THIS CLOSELY 👀

Leadership succession had become an important overhang for Kotak Mahindra Bank.

When Vaswani announced in June that he would not seek reappointment, Kotak shares fell more than 2% as investors assessed the uncertainty around his successor.

The RBI's approval of an internal candidate now removes a major part of that uncertainty.

Importantly, Saha isn't joining Kotak from outside on January 1.

He is already part of the bank's senior leadership team and has been overseeing major customer-facing businesses, potentially allowing for a smoother transition.

KEY TAKEAWAY 📌

The significance of this announcement goes beyond today's 3% stock move.

Kotak Mahindra Bank is moving from succession uncertainty to a clearly defined leadership transition.

Saha's background also provides clues about areas that could remain important under his leadership:

Retail banking, customer acquisition, digital transformation, analytics and execution.

However, the appointment itself doesn't change Kotak's fundamentals overnight.

WHAT TO WATCH 👀

The bigger questions will be how Kotak performs under the transition across:

🔹 Deposit growth
🔹 Loan growth
🔹 CASA franchise
🔹 Net interest margins
🔹 Retail banking
🔹 Digital customer acquisition
🔹 Asset quality
🔹 Return on equity
🔹 Execution of the bank's existing strategy

For investors tracking the banking sector, leadership uncertainty at Kotak has now reduced considerably.

The next phase will be about execution.

9 investments. 9 different stories. 
9 convictions worth questioning.

“KKR exited” sounds like useful information.

But without knowing why KKR entered, what changed while it owned the stake, and why it eventually sold, it tells us surprisingly little.

The image shows the returns.
The stories are more interesting.

1. CGPOWER | The investment KKR never really chose

KKR did not enter CG Power as a conventional PE bet.

In September 2019, KKR’s credit entities ended up with ~10% of CG Power at ₹14.25/share by enforcing pledged shares against loans made to the promoter group.

And look at the situation then.

CG Power had just disclosed serious accounting and governance irregularities. 

Liabilities had been understated, related-party transactions were under investigation, operations were deteriorating and lenders were looking for a resolution.

So KKR’s “thesis” here was primarily credit recovery, not:
Power equipment is going to boom.

KKR sold during 2020.

Then Murugappa Group entered through Tube Investments, repaired the balance sheet, restored governance and rebuilt the operating business.

Today, the backdrop could barely look more different.

India is in another large transmission/grid-capex cycle, driven by electrification and renewable integration.

CG Power has also added an entirely new semiconductor adjacency through CG Semi, whose first facility started commercial production in 2026.

Post-KKR reference return: ~51x.

Questioning the conviction:
Can a terrible company situation temporarily hide a very good underlying industrial asset?

2. MAXHEALTH | Consolidation before healthcare became fashionable

KKR-backed Radiant moved on Max Healthcare in 2018.

The thesis was unusually explicit:
scale + consolidation + cost synergies + margin improvement + growing demand for quality healthcare.

The merger created one of India's largest hospital networks, with more than 3,200 beds at the time, and KKR specifically highlighted the ability to use the platform for further healthcare consolidation.

KKR eventually made roughly 5x and exited.

But that did not mean India's hospital runway had ended.

Max today operates 6,100+ beds, while large Indian hospital operators continued delivering >15% revenue and EBITDA growth in FY26 amid further capacity build-out.

Post-KKR: ~2.83x.

Questioning the conviction:
When PE has already made 5x, has the opportunity matured, or has the company merely moved from turnaround → scale → compounding?

P.S: I personally stay away from direct investments in healthcare sector.

3. POONAWALLA | Magma was originally a financial-inclusion bet

Go back to 2011.

Magma was not today's Poonawalla Fincorp.

It was an NBFC heavily exposed to rural and semi-urban India, financing commercial vehicles, construction equipment, tractors, cars and SMEs.

Around 80% of its branches were in rural/semi-urban markets.

I could not find a clean public KKR statement spelling out its exact thesis, but the contemporaneous investment documents make the likely thesis fairly clear:
underserved credit + branch expansion + product expansion + financial inclusion.

KKR exited around 2018 at roughly 2x.

Then the company itself changed.

New promoter. New balance sheet.
New distribution. New products. 
New underwriting architecture.

By FY26, Poonawalla Fincorp had ₹60,348 Cr AUM, up 69.4%, with a much broader mix across secured and unsecured products.

Post-KKR: ~2.68x.

Questioning the conviction:
In lending, what is the real moat?
Distribution? Cost of capital? 
Underwriting? Or the ability to reinvent all three?

4. MFSL | KKR explicitly bet on financialisation

KKR bought 9.95% of Max Financial in 2016 just after the Max Group demerger created a clean listed life-insurance vehicle.

KKR's rationale was explicit:
India's growth, increasing financial savings, and the resulting growth of the life-insurance industry.

That structural thesis largely played out.

But today's question is different.

IRDAI is now proposing another reset of insurance distribution economics, including tighter commission and expense structures.

Post-KKR reference: ~+120%.

Questioning the conviction:
If insurance penetration remains low but distribution economics change, who captures the next decade's value: bank, agent or platform?

5. SBILIFE | Distribution itself was an asset
KKR entered SBI Life in December 2016 at ₹460/share, shortly before its IPO.

The attraction was difficult to miss.

SBI Life combined a leading private insurer with access to the enormous SBI distribution network. 

Contemporary analysis highlighted its profitability, product mix and reach through SBI's banking franchise.

KKR subsequently monetised through multiple transactions.

Post-KKR reference: ~+77%.

Now the same industry faces a new question as regulators try to lower distribution costs.

Questioning the conviction:
In insurance, is a giant distribution network always an advantage, or does its value change when commissions themselves are regulated downward?

6. DALBHARAT | KKR bought cement when everyone could see oversupply

In 2010, Indian cement was dealing with massive capacity additions, falling utilisation and pricing pressure, particularly in southern India. Industry utilisation had already fallen sharply as new supply entered.

And KKR invested ₹750 Cr into Dalmia.

Why?
The money was explicitly meant for:
organic growth + inorganic growth + deleveraging.

Dalmia was restructuring itself into a focused cement platform, had reached 9 MTPA capacity and was planning another 10 MTPA of greenfield projects.

KKR eventually made 3.6x.

Post-KKR: ~+61%.

Questioning the conviction:
Is industry overcapacity always bearish?

Or can the weak part of a cycle actually be the best time for a low-cost player with capital to build capacity?

7. HDFCBANK | KKR wasn't just buying a mortgage lender

KKR invested in HDFC Ltd in early 2018.

But look at what the fresh capital was meant for:

→ maintain HDFC's stake in HDFC Bank
→ health-insurance opportunities
→ stressed real-estate assets
→ affordable housing
→ funding subsidiaries

It was effectively backing a capital-allocation platform, not merely a home-loan book.

Then came the NBFC liquidity crisis.

Years later came the HDFC Ltd + HDFC Bank merger.

KKR itself had already exited with roughly a 15% gain.

Post-KKR equivalent price return: ~+22%.

Questioning the conviction:
Was HDFC's historical moat the mortgage product itself, or the ecosystem, funding advantage and capital allocation around it?

That distinction matters even more after the merger.

8. COFFEEDAY | Right consumption thesis. Wrong balance-sheet outcome.

In 2010, KKR called Café Coffee Day a fast-growing retailer.

The consumer story was obvious.

India's organised retail market was expanding rapidly, CCD had built enormous brand recognition, and cafés were becoming part of urban India's changing consumption habits.

But KKR wasn't buying only a coffee shop.

The holding company also contained several other businesses, including real estate/infrastructure-related assets.

KKR monetised some shares at much higher prices, but remained invested while leverage and corporate complexity overwhelmed the consumer story.

Its eventual overall outcome was only around 1.2x.

Questioning the conviction:
Can you be completely right about the consumer trend and still lose because the capital structure is wrong?

Brand ≠ balance sheet.

9. INDUSTOWER | Telecom grew. The tower stock didn't compound accordingly.

KKR invested $250m in Bharti Infratel in 2008.
The setup was compelling.

India was adding telecom subscribers rapidly. Operators were expanding into new geographies. 

Sharing passive infrastructure allowed faster rollouts and better economics.

The tower model had significant operating leverage because each additional tenant could improve returns on an already-built asset.

KKR eventually made roughly 1.8x.

Yet the successor Indus Towers has delivered roughly flat-to-negative price returns from our exit reference, excluding substantial dividends.

Meanwhile the underlying infrastructure never became irrelevant.

Indus is still adding towers and co-locations, has 563,000 installed 5G BTSs, and its tenancy ratio stands around 1.62.

Questioning the conviction:
Can an industry experience exponential data growth while the infrastructure owner still delivers mediocre stock returns?

Absolutely.

Demand growth ≠ shareholder returns.
And that connects all nine stories.

KKR exiting is an event.
It is not an investment thesis.

PE investors have fund lives, return hurdles and liquidity constraints.

They also often own meaningful blocks.

So exits commonly happen through multiple block/bulk/open-market transactions, sometimes spread across months or years.

More importantly, KKR's investment objective and your investment objective can be completely different.

The better questions are:

Why did they enter?
What changed while they were there?
Why are they exiting?

And which part of the original thesis still has runway after they leave?

That, to me, is a much better way to exercise the #QuestioningConvictionMuscle than blindly following “smart money.”

Kalyan Jewellers India shares gained around 2.5% to ₹578 in early trade on September 29, outperforming a weak broader market after UBS reiterated its Buy rating on the jewellery retailer.

🔹 Stock price: ~₹578
🔹 Early gain: ~2.5%
🔹 Previous close: ₹564
🔹 2026 YTD gain: ~19%
🔹 Market cap: ~₹59,600 Cr
🔹 UBS target price: ₹900
🔹 Implied upside from previous close: ~60%

The ₹900 target and Buy rating are UBS's estimates, not our recommendation.

WHY IS UBS POSITIVE? 📈

Following interactions with Kalyan Jewellers' management, UBS highlighted expectations of stronger growth during the second half of the current financial year despite a high base.

Key factors highlighted include:

🔹 Stronger H2 growth outlook
🔹 Continued aggressive store expansion
🔹 Visibility from gold savings schemes
🔹 Capital-light expansion through the FOCO model
🔹 Long-term opportunity from organised jewellery gaining market share

GOLD PRICES REMAIN AN IMPORTANT VARIABLE 🪙

Management indicated that elevated gold prices are affecting customer segments differently.

Higher gold prices can influence:

🔹 Jewellery demand
🔹 Average ticket sizes
🔹 Consumer purchasing behaviour
🔹 Product mix

However, UBS believes Kalyan's growth can continue to be supported by network expansion and market-share gains.

AGGRESSIVE STORE EXPANSION 🏬

UBS had initiated coverage on Kalyan Jewellers earlier this month with the same ₹900 target.

The brokerage highlighted the company's franchise-owned, company-operated model as an important driver of capital-efficient expansion.

UBS also noted that Kalyan's pace of store additions has been nearly twice that of Titan.

GROWTH TRACK RECORD 📊

According to UBS:

🔹 Revenue CAGR FY22-FY26: ~35%
🔹 Expected revenue CAGR over next 5 years: ~23%
🔹 Expected earnings CAGR over next 5 years: ~23%

The brokerage also estimates Kalyan trades at around 30x FY28 earnings, representing roughly a 45% discount to Titan.

KEY TAKEAWAY 📌

Kalyan Jewellers' move stands out because it came while the broader market was under pressure.

The UBS thesis is primarily built around continued store expansion, the capital-light FOCO model, market-share gains and expectations of strong revenue and earnings growth.

The stock's ~19% gain in 2026 also contrasts with the Nifty 50's double-digit decline over the same period.

WHAT TO WATCH 👀

H2 same-store sales growth, new store additions, franchise economics, margins and the impact of elevated gold prices on consumer demand will remain important operating monitorables.

Execution becomes particularly important given the company's rapid network expansion and the growth expectations embedded in brokerage estimates.

India installed 8.2 GWh of grid batteries in the first half of 2026.

Nearly every cell inside them was imported.

Why does that matter?

Look at the demand side.
H1 2025: 98 MWh of battery storage installed.
H1 2026: 8.2 GWh.

That's 84 times in one year.
Crisil expects another 45 to 50 GWh to be commissioned across FY27 and FY28. Wood Mackenzie puts India's storage tender pipeline at 260 GWh.

Now the supply side.
In August, Wood Mackenzie counted 2 GWh of operational cell capacity in India. That's enough to meet less than 1% of the pipeline. Even with Exide's new 6 GWh line, which isn't in commercial production yet, domestic supply is a small fraction of what's coming.

So the gap gets filled by imports.
🔹 Li-ion battery imports in FY26: $4.7 bn, up 57%
🔹 Share from China: 83.6%

And this isn't just a trade deficit number. It shows up in P&Ls.

Chinese storage cell prices rose 22% in six months. Crisil says battery costs went from $50 to 55/kWh in 2025 to $70 to 75/kWh in 2026.

Developers usually buy batteries about a year after winning a bid. So projects won at 2025 tariffs are now paying 2026 prices. Crisil flags 12 GWh of capacity with weak returns.

When one country supplies your cells, it also sets your margins.

That's why local manufacturing matters.  For pricing power.

India has announced 226 GWh of cell capacity through 2035. 

Here's the part most people miss.
In July 2025, Beijing added LFP cathode technology to its restricted-export list. Taking it out of China now needs a licence.

On paper, that covers one material. On the ground, Indian companies are telling a very different story.

Amara Raja signed a licence with Gotion's European arm in 2024. It never moved. The company is now building its own tech, and its new-energy head says sharing is "largely discouraged by the Chinese government."

Then came the part that made me stop.

This week, Advait signed to buy up to 1 GWh of cells from China's Hithium. Back in January, Bloomberg reported that Hithium wouldn't license its LFP tech to Reliance. Reliance denied it.

So China will sell India the cell. Just not the recipe.

JSW has stopped waiting for it.

Last week, chairman Sajjan Jindal called the cell "the new oil" and said China will supply cells but won't share the know-how. His own estimate for building the technology in-house: one to two years, if things go well.

Also, JSW Projects and COEP Tech announced a battery R&D centre in Pune, with over ₹800 crore committed across two phases. Phase 1 will design and prototype lithium-ion and sodium-ion cells. Phase 2 is a validation centre able to produce cells from 100 to 600 Ah.

And Exide? Its 6 GWh plant was commissioned last week on SVOLT technology. But that deal was signed in March 2022, three years before the door closed.

Where India's own effort stands:
🔹 PLI ACC scheme: 40 GWh awarded, ~1.4 GWh operational, zero incentives paid as of Feb 2026
🔹 Ola Electric: 2.5 GWh operational, in-house technology
🔹 Amara Raja: first 2 GWh line targeted for 2027
🔹 Agratas (Tata): 20 GWh at Sanand, first equipment arrived this month, output in 2027

If the lock sits on the cathode, the materials layer is where it gets interesting:
🔹 Gujarat Fluorochemicals: supplying LiPF6 commercially since Dec 2025. LFP cathode final qualification expected by Q3 FY27
🔹 Himadri Speciality: 40,000 tpa LFP cathode in Phase I, first 2,000 tpa by Q3 FY27
🔹 Neogen Chemicals: ₹1,795 cr battery-chemicals capex, electrolyte production in H1 FY27

🔸 The other side: restricted is not banned, and licences can still be granted. Home-grown cells cost 25 to 40% more than imports. 

And China's wider controls on anode, cathode and cell-making equipment are only suspended, until 10 Nov 2026.

India can announce gigawatts. Buying the recipe is getting harder.

Why interest rates and earnings growth matter so much when judging index valuations.
To understand this more applicable way is to look at Nifty valuation is through the "equity risk premium" ! 
At around 19–20x PE, Nifty earnings yield is roughly 5–5.2%.
India’s 10-year bond yield is around 6–7%.
So purely on current yield, equities are not giving you any obvious premium over bonds, & the extra return has to come from future earnings growth.
If Nifty earnings grow 12–14% for the next few years, this can still work well because your earnings base keeps expanding, but if earnings growth drops to 6–8%, suddenly the present valuation starts looking far less attractive.
